title: Positive trigonometric averages turn a nearby zero into a one-sided obstruction
claim: Both arguments combine logarithmic-derivative values with a nonnegative trigonometric weight so that the Euler-product side is nonnegative while a hypothesized nearby zero contributes a reciprocal-distance term. Stechkin symmetrization sharpens this architecture by pairing each zero with its functional-equation partner and shifting the logarithmic derivative, which makes noncandidate zero pairs discardable before the candidate is bounded.
historical_or_program_relation: The Stechkin–Kadiri framework refines the classical positivity proof of zero repulsion by adding a symmetry-aware shifted comparison rather than changing the underlying prime-side positivity mechanism.
limits: The two units use different growth inputs, radii, normalizations, and admissible weights; they establish zero-free boundaries near the one-line, not critical-line location or RH, and neither unit alone supplies a globally optimal boundary.

title: Zero-free optimization must preserve admissibility and score the actual region objective
claim: Across kernel and trigonometric-polynomial searches, the candidate representation is useful only after it is mapped through the full certified zero-free argument: kernel conditions and monotonicity are rechecked for each h-family, while an autocorrelation factorization makes trigonometric nonnegativity automatic. The observed reversal between Landau's surrogate ranking and the finite R0 ranking shows why admissibility-preserving search must be followed by task-specific evaluation.
historical_or_program_relation: The program evolves from comparing a few explicit test kernels, through large surrogate-guided polynomial searches with downstream reranking, to a factorized search coordinate that enforces positivity identically.
limits: The 2014 and 2015 units optimize a classical logarithmic region constant, whereas the 2024 autocorrelation unit targets an asymptotic Vinogradov–Korobov constant; their numerical objectives are not interchangeable, and heuristic or local search does not certify a global optimum.

title: Explicit zero-free proofs splice a finite zero certificate to analytic tail control
claim: A verified low-zero range removes candidate zeros below a cutoff so the rescaled positivity argument can be uniform above it; complementary reciprocal-square or zero-count estimates compress the unenumerated zeros into a controlled aggregate tail. Thus finite computation and global analysis meet at an explicit cutoff rather than one replacing the other.
historical_or_program_relation: The newer explicit-region pipeline updates the finite verification anchor, while later treatments retain the same splice and strengthen the analytic side with uniform N(T) error bounds for remote-zero detector terms.
limits: Finite verification below T0 is an external dependency and does not prove RH beyond that height; aggregate tail bounds do not locate individual zeros, and every cutoff, completeness claim, test-function hypothesis, and height range must remain attached to its source.

title: Contour optimization transports zero-free geometry into distinct prime-counting error scales
claim: The boundary of a zero-free region is a reusable input to the prime-number-theorem contour: a classical width 1/(R log t) yields square-root-exponential decay whose constants improve with R, while the wider Vinogradov–Korobov boundary yields the different exponent exp(-c(log x)^(3/5)/(log log x)^(1/5)) after optimizing contour height.
historical_or_program_relation: Explicit classical-region work progressively improves finite constants and downstream explicit inequalities, whereas the Vinogradov–Korobov program changes the asymptotic shape of the available contour shift by importing exponential-sum cancellation.
limits: The sources use different prime-counting functions, explicit ranges, and auxiliary estimates, so constants cannot be transferred by substitution without rechecking those inputs; improving classical R does not by itself improve the Vinogradov–Korobov exponent, and neither error term implies RH-scale square-root cancellation.

title: Exponential-sum cancellation changes the asymptotic zero-free envelope through a zeta bound
claim: Taylor polynomialization, Hölder amplification, and Vinogradov mean values produce cancellation in short sums of n^(-it); blockwise Abel summation then transfers that local cancellation to a bound for zeta near the one-line. The resulting input supports a Vinogradov–Korobov boundary, which is naturally compared with classical regions as a height-dependent envelope rather than by a constant alone.
historical_or_program_relation: This identifies the analytic route behind the asymptotic-shape improvement: exponential-sum structure changes the zeta growth bound, and only then changes the zero-free envelope used in later explicit comparisons.
limits: The lecture-note estimate suppresses explicit constants, while an asymptotically superior envelope can lose on finite height ranges; the chain supplies no zero-free continuation to the critical line and gives no RH inference.

title: Zero-detecting polynomials produce density bounds that later create usable zero-free intervals
claim: A zero is first converted into a large Dirichlet-polynomial value, with powering used to match the witness length to a Halász–Montgomery, reflection, and fourth-moment large-value theorem; the resulting density estimate can then bound contaminated t-blocks. Excising those blocks creates long retained intervals where a logarithmic branch exists and a Mellin-smoothed Dirichlet polynomial recovers mean-square coefficient mass.
historical_or_program_relation: The density theorem is not merely an endpoint count: in the mean-value argument it becomes an upstream resource that converts sparse zero information into a geometric domain on which finite polynomial approximation is valid.
limits: The producer treats families of L-functions while the consumer is formulated for a particular Dirichlet-series setting, so exponents and hypotheses are not directly transferable; excision loses bad blocks and edge regions, gives no everywhere-in-t zero-free region, and the scanned formulas are too damaged to support new exact constants.

title: Critical-line proportions are optimized only after zero counting is compressed to a mollified mean square
claim: The argument principle and Littlewood's lemma replace direct critical-line zero counting by a shifted mean square of a mollified differential combination. In the earlier formulation this mean becomes a quadratic functional whose relaxed optimizer solves an Euler–Lagrange boundary problem; the later three-piece mollifier expands the same optimization interface into six diagonal and cross moments and compresses them to a scalar c governing the proportion bound.
historical_or_program_relation: The later construction refines the admissible mollifier representation and moment bookkeeping while preserving the earlier proof architecture from argument variation to mollified norm to numerical optimization.
limits: The two mean-value theorems have different length restrictions, smoothing steps, and multiplicity conventions; polynomial approximation and displayed numerical witnesses do not prove global optimality, and a positive critical-line proportion is not RH.

title: Critical-line sign changes become a finite completeness certificate only when matched to a total zero count
claim: Sign changes of the real critical-line Z-function provide local lower bounds on critical-line zeros, while an independent argument-principle count supplies the total number of zeros in a bounded rectangle. Equality of those counts closes the location gap; later Gram-block search strategies reduce the cost of finding the required sign changes without changing that proof object.
historical_or_program_relation: The computational program separates certification from search efficiency: early work combined sign changes with Backlund counting, and later work optimized where Z is evaluated while retaining the need for a sufficient count.
limits: Gram's one-zero-per-interval law has failures and is not itself a completeness theorem; the conclusion is bounded by the certified height and rectangle, depends on rigorous sign and total-count error control, and cannot be extrapolated to global RH.
